case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a Tax Court proceeding under 26 U.S.C. § 6330 challenging a proposed IRS levy becomes moot once the IRS no longer seeks that levy (because it collected the money through offsets or otherwise), even though the parties still dispute the taxpayer’s entitlement to the funds.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 26 U.S.C. § 6330 (Collection Due Process procedures and Tax Court review), especially § 6330(d)(1) (judicial review) and § 6330(e)(1) (suspension of levy/injunctive authority); related remedial/justiciability constraints (mootness under Article III) and interaction arguments involving the Declaratory Judgment Act’s tax exception (as discussed by respondent).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Commissioner argues the case is moot because § 6330 is designed to provide a pre-deprivation review of a specific proposed levy, and once the IRS is no longer pursuing that levy there is no longer a live dispute for the Tax Court to resolve. In the government’s view, Tax Court jurisdiction under § 6330 is tied to the existence of an active levy controversy; allowing the case to continue would improperly convert § 6330 into a broad vehicle to litigate underlying liability or payment/credit issues (including offsets) outside the traditional refund-suit framework, thereby expanding Tax Court jurisdiction beyond what Congress authorized. The government also contends the Tax Court lacks implicit authority in a § 6330 case to review offsets or to grant declaratory-type relief about entitlement to disputed funds once levy collection is off the table.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Zuch argues the case is not moot because the parties still have concrete stakes: who is legally entitled to the disputed payments/credits the IRS retained. She contends § 6330(d)(1)’s grant of Tax Court jurisdiction is triggered by the Appeals determination and does not evaporate merely because the IRS later stops pursuing the levy, especially where the taxpayer’s 'unpaid tax' and 'underlying liability' remain contested. She also argues the Tax Court can issue effective relief by deciding those issues and entering a judgment that changes the parties’ legal rights, which would (i) materially increase the likelihood of a refund and/or (ii) have issue-preclusive effect in a refund suit under § 7422 (which she has filed). Respondent further maintains § 6330(e)(1) confirms meaningful remedial authority (including injunctions and, functionally, declaratory determinations within the CDP framework), and that the government’s mootness theory would let the IRS strategically moot CDP cases by switching collection mechanisms after the taxpayer invokes review.
key_precedents: Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020)
Medtronic, Inc. v. Mirowski Family Ventures, LLC, 571 U.S. 191 (2014)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that § 6330(e)(1) is levy-specific and that CDP review should not be transmuted into a general refund forum; I agree with that structural caution and would keep our holding narrow. But their mootness conclusion still runs into Chafin/Knox: where the taxpayer timely raised the existence/amount of the “unpaid tax” (including credits/payments) for the same period, a judgment vacating the Appeals “determination” on that ground alters the parties’ legal relations regarding whether the Government may lawfully retain offsets applied to satisfy that asserted liability, which is more than mere preclusion value. Reed v. Goertz, as Justice Barrett invokes it, properly rejects jurisdiction based solely on the collateral utility of a decision, but here the remaining stake is the Government’s present entitlement to money already taken under the very liability premise the determination embodies, and Friends of the Earth counsels against permitting strategic mooting by switching collection tools midstream. A minimalist disposition can recognize redressability only in this tight category without expanding Tax Court power to order refunds or to adjudicate unrelated periods.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s argument that vacating the Appeals “determination” would concretely affect the Government’s ability to retain offsets still assumes a form of relief that this § 6330(d)(1) cause of action authorizes after the noticed levy is abandoned. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, § 6330’s structure—especially § 6330(e)(1)’s levy-specific stay—confirms Congress keyed CDP review to whether a particular levy may proceed, not to adjudicating entitlement to amounts already collected by offset, which Congress channeled through the refund scheme. Reed v. Goertz reinforces (rather than undermines) that redressability must come from relief the court can award “in the case,” and a decision valued chiefly for downstream leverage or preclusion in § 7422 litigation does not suffice. Laidlaw/voluntary-cessation concerns raised by Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan are policy-serious, but they cannot expand jurisdiction beyond the statute’s original public meaning where the challenged levy has ended and the remaining dispute is, in substance, a refund/credit controversy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that, under Chafin/Knox and voluntary-cessation principles, vacating the Appeals “determination” could meaningfully affect whether the Government may retain the offsets already applied. But that assumes the Tax Court, in a § 6330(d)(1) CDP case, has remedial authority to alter the parties’ legal position regarding money collected by offset; § 6330(e)(1)’s levy-only stay and the levy-centered structure suggest Congress did not create a freestanding forum to adjudicate entitlement to credits/refunds once collection proceeds by other means. Reed v. Goertz reinforces (as Justice Barrett emphasizes) that redressability must come from relief available “in the case,” not from the hoped-for downstream utility of a merits ruling in separate § 7422 refund/offset litigation. Laidlaw’s strategic-mooting concerns are real, but they cannot justify expanding Tax Court jurisdiction beyond the text Congress wrote in § 6330 and the longstanding channeling of post-collection money disputes into the refund scheme.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point—that § 6330 is levy-centered and § 6330(e)(1) stays only levy action—goes to the scope of statutory remedies, but it does not carry the Article III mootness question when a court can still grant effectual relief by setting aside the Appeals “determination” that there is an “unpaid tax.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, that determination is the legal premise the Government invokes to justify retaining the offsets already taken, so vacatur or reversal on the credit/payment issue changes the parties’ concrete legal positions even if the Tax Court cannot itself order a refund. Reed v. Goertz, properly read, rejects redressability based on “preclusion value alone,” but it does not require that the only permissible relief be an injunction against the precise collection tool initially noticed; it requires a judgment with real-world legal consequences, which exists here. And Justice Jackson’s voluntary-cessation concern matters in practice: allowing the IRS to moot CDP review by swapping from levy to offset would predictably burden low-income taxpayers by forcing them into more complex refund litigation, undermining Congress’s access-to-justice design.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s strongest point—that § 6330(e)(1) stays only “levy” activity and Reed v. Goertz rejects jurisdiction premised on mere preclusion value—does not, in my view, carry the mootness argument because § 6330(d)(1) authorizes review of the Appeals “determination,” and vacating that determination on the ground that the tax was not “unpaid” (because credits satisfied it) changes the parties’ legal relationship as to the Government’s asserted basis for retaining what it collected. Reed matters, but I read it alongside Chafin/Knox to require effectual relief in the real world, not necessarily an order compelling immediate repayment; here the relief is undoing the operative administrative determination that purports to justify collection for that period. Chief Justice Roberts’s framing is persuasive to me: a narrow holding limited to properly raised underlying-liability/credit issues avoids converting CDP into a refund forum while preventing an administratively simple end-run where the IRS moots congressionally provided review by switching from levy to offsets midstream. Justice Alito’s remedial-structure concern is serious, but under a pragmatic textualist reading it is more coherent to treat the “determination” as the reviewable object even if the collection tool changes, rather than making CDP review strategically evadable.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Sotomayor’s “effectual relief” account depends on treating a merits judgment about “unpaid tax” as altering the Government’s right to retain offsets, but that relief is not one the Tax Court is authorized to award in this § 6330(d)(1) CDP proceeding once the proposed levy is withdrawn. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, § 6330(e)(1) stays only levy action and the statute’s remedial structure is keyed to whether a noticed levy may proceed; using the “determination” language to reach offsets would effectively convert CDP review into a refund/credit adjudication Congress channeled through § 7422. Reed v. Goertz reinforces that redressability must come from relief available “in the case,” not from preclusion leverage or a declaration designed to drive different litigation, and Laidlaw’s voluntary-cessation concern cannot justify expanding jurisdiction beyond the statute’s original public meaning and separation-of-powers limits. I therefore remain with Petitioner on mootness in this posture, while acknowledging (as Justice Jackson notes) that any strategic-mooting problem is for Congress to cure by authorizing an offsets remedy in CDP.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s point (echoed by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan) that vacating the Appeals “determination” could affect the Government’s entitlement to retain offsets is the strongest argument against mootness, and it appropriately invokes Chafin/Knox and voluntary-cessation concerns. But under Reed v. Goertz, redressability still turns on whether the court can grant effectual relief within the cause of action Congress actually created; here, as Justice Barrett emphasizes, § 6330(e)(1) suspends only levy activity and § 6330(d)(1) review is structured around whether a noticed levy may proceed, not around adjudicating entitlement to already-applied offsets. Treating a merits ruling on “unpaid tax” as effectual relief as to offsets effectively collapses the longstanding statutory division between CDP review and § 7422 refund litigation, expanding Tax Court jurisdiction by implication rather than text, history, and traditional remedial channels. Voluntary-cessation is a real institutional concern, but it should be handled through orthodox mootness exceptions when recurrence is likely, not by recharacterizing CDP as a forum for retention-of-offsets disputes once the levy is withdrawn.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Sotomayor’s point that, under Chafin/Knox and Laidlaw, a case is not moot if a court can still grant effectual relief that alters legal rights, and I agree we should not invite strategic mooting. But Reed v. Goertz reinforces that redressability must come from relief the court may award in this case, and § 6330’s text and remedial structure—especially § 6330(e)(1)’s levy-specific stay—tie CDP review to whether a proposed levy may proceed, not to adjudicating the Government’s entitlement to funds already collected through offsets. The respondents’ “retention of offsets” theory depends on treating § 6330(d)(1)’s review of the “determination” as a freestanding merits forum after the levy is withdrawn, which would expand Tax Court jurisdiction by implication and erode the statutory line Congress drew between CDP and refund/credit litigation under § 7422. Voluntary-cessation concerns do not justify that jurisdictional expansion where the challenged action is the discrete levy noticed and then abandoned; any remaining benefit from a merits ruling is essentially collateral to the cause of action Congress created.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is that § 6330 is levy-centered and that § 6330(e)(1) stays only a levy, so the Tax Court cannot itself order a refund of offsets in this posture; that statutory remedial limit is real. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor emphasize, Article III mootness turns on whether the judgment can still alter the parties’ legal rights in a concrete way, and vacating or setting aside an Appeals “determination” premised on an “unpaid tax” (when the taxpayer properly raised payment/credit issues) changes the Government’s lawful entitlement to retain amounts collected to satisfy that very asserted liability—it is more than “preclusion value” in a separate § 7422 suit. Reed v. Goertz, properly understood, requires redressability through effectual change in legal position, not necessarily immediate money-in-hand, and allowing the IRS to moot CDP review by switching from levy to offset after a petition is filed would invite strategic behavior in tension with Laidlaw’s voluntary-cessation principles and Congress’s procedural-fairness design. On a pragmatic reading attentive to consequences, keeping jurisdiction here does not convert CDP into a general refund forum; it simply preserves review of the still-live liability/payment premise embedded in the challenged determination for the same tax period.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Article III, a case is moot only when it is “impossible for a court to grant any effectual relief whatever” to the prevailing party, and even a small concrete stake suffices. Knox v. Serv. Emps. Int’l Union, 567 U.S. 298, 307 (2012); Chafin v. Chafin, 568 U.S. 165, 172 (2013). Here, a § 6330(d)(1) petition challenges the Appeals determination, and the dispute over whether the taxpayer’s “underlying liability” remains unpaid (and thus whether the Government may retain the offsets) can still yield effectual relief by altering the parties’ legal rights and preventing strategic mooting through unilateral collection choices, consistent with voluntary-cessation principles. Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw, 528 U.S. 167, 189 (2000). A narrow holding that the case is not moot so long as the taxpayer contests liability/credits tied to the challenged collection determination preserves institutional legitimacy by avoiding an overbroad expansion of Tax Court remedial power while enforcing Article III’s settled “effectual relief” standard.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 6330 establishes a narrow, levy-focused procedure: it authorizes review of the IRS’s determination to proceed with a specific levy and stays that levy during review, see 26 U.S.C. § 6330(d)(1), (e)(1). Once the Government is no longer pursuing the challenged levy because the amount has been collected through offsets or otherwise, there is no longer any effectual relief the Tax Court can grant within the statutory confines of § 6330; continuing would improperly convert CDP review into a vehicle for adjudicating entitlement to funds or credits—a function Congress has channeled into refund litigation under § 7422. Article III mootness principles confirm that a case is moot when the court cannot grant effectual relief, Knox v. SEIU, 567 U.S. 298, 307 (2012), and mere potential issue-preclusive value in separate litigation does not supply jurisdiction absent a live levy controversy. The text and structure of § 6330 thus counsel dismissing as moot when the levy dispute has ceased, regardless of remaining disagreements about ultimate entitlement to the money.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 6330 is structured as a focused, pre-deprivation check on a specific proposed levy, and the Tax Court’s review under § 6330(d)(1) is properly understood as tethered to whether that levy remains a live collection action that the court can restrain under § 6330(e)(1). Once the IRS is no longer pursuing the levy and the money has been collected through offsets or other means, the court cannot grant “effectual relief” with respect to the challenged levy, rendering the case moot under Article III. Allowing continued litigation merely to obtain a merits ruling with potential issue-preclusive effect in a separate refund suit would expand CDP into a broad vehicle for adjudicating payment/credit disputes beyond the limited remedy Congress provided, contrary to the practical consequences and jurisdictional limits implied by the statute. Reed v. Goertz and Knox underscore that mootness turns on whether the court can still provide concrete relief in the case at hand, not whether a party would benefit from a favorable decision in later litigation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A § 6330(d)(1) CDP case is not moot simply because the IRS has stopped pursuing the specific levy, where the parties still dispute the taxpayer’s entitlement to the retained funds and the court can grant effectual relief by resolving the contested “underlying liability” and “unpaid tax” issues. Under Article III, a case becomes moot only when it is impossible to grant any effectual relief, and a judgment that changes the parties’ legal status and materially increases the likelihood of relief—either through the IRS’s compliance or through issue preclusion in a pending refund suit—suffices. Reed v. Goertz and Medtronic confirm that relief need not be immediate cash-in-hand to be effectual, and Herrera underscores that issue preclusion is a concrete legal consequence of a valid judgment. Reading mootness as the Commissioner urges would invite strategic mooting by shifting from a levy to offsets after a taxpayer invokes § 6330 review, undermining Congress’s protective CDP framework and § 6330(e)(1)’s contemplated remedial authority.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: A § 6330(d)(1) petition seeks review of the Appeals determination, and Article III mootness turns on whether the parties retain a concrete stake, not on whether the IRS later shifts collection tools; here the entitlement-to-funds/underlying-liability dispute remains live, and the court can still grant effective relief by resolving those issues within the CDP framework. Under Reed v. Goertz, a case is not moot so long as a court can grant relief that matters in the real world, even if it is limited (including determining legal rights that materially affect the taxpayer’s position in ongoing refund litigation). Treating the case as moot whenever the IRS ceases the levy would invite unilateral action to defeat judicial review, contrary to the voluntary-cessation principle (Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw) and would undercut § 6330(e)(1)’s design to make CDP review workable by preventing end-runs around the statutory process. The government’s jurisdictional narrowing reads § 6330’s remedial scheme too grudgingly given Congress’s evident aim of coherent, reviewable collection procedures rather than a moving-target regime dependent on the IRS’s post-petition choices.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 6330 is textually framed around review of a specific “proposed levy” and the Appeals “determination” whether that levy may proceed, with § 6330(e)(1) suspending only levy action—not other collection tools like offsets—so once the IRS is no longer seeking the levy, the court cannot grant effectual relief within the statutory cause of action. Whatever dispute remains about entitlement to the funds is, in substance, a payment/refund controversy Congress channeled to the refund-suit scheme (e.g., § 7422), and we should not expand the Tax Court’s limited jurisdiction by implication. Unlike Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw, this is not voluntary cessation of the challenged conduct with a likelihood of recurrence; the challenged levy has ended and a CDP case cannot be converted into freestanding declaratory relief about credits. Under Article III mootness principles, a case is moot when the court can no longer “grant any effectual relief whatever,” and that is so here given the narrow remedial structure of § 6330 and separation-of-powers limits on judicially enlarging Tax Court authority.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A § 6330(d)(1) CDP case is structured as judicial review of an Appeals determination concerning a proposed levy, and § 6330(e)(1)’s suspension/injunctive mechanism confirms that the central remedial focus is stopping or conditioning that levy, not adjudicating post-collection entitlement to funds. Once the IRS is no longer pursuing the challenged levy and the Tax Court cannot grant effectual relief directed to that levy, Article III mootness principles counsel dismissal because the remaining dispute over credits/offsets belongs in the traditional refund-suit framework under § 7422, not as de facto declaratory relief in Tax Court. The Court’s mootness cases emphasize that a dispute becomes moot when it is impossible to grant effectual relief (Knox v. SEIU), and extending § 6330 beyond its text and historic function would expand Tax Court jurisdiction in a way Congress did not clearly authorize. Any concern about strategic agency behavior is better addressed by Congress or by applying established exceptions only where truly necessary, rather than converting CDP review into a general vehicle for payment/credit litigation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Article III requires a live controversy and effective relief; § 6330 is textually structured around review of a "proposed levy" and an Appeals "determination" about whether that levy may proceed, with § 6330(e)(1) suspending or enjoining the levy—not adjudicating entitlement to funds already collected by other means. Once the IRS is no longer seeking the levy challenged in the CDP notice, the Tax Court cannot grant levy-focused relief, and a taxpayer’s interest in a favorable ruling for possible downstream advantages (including potential issue-preclusion in a separate § 7422 refund suit) does not by itself supply redressability under Reed v. Goertz. Allowing continuation would expand § 6330(d)(1) beyond its original public meaning and Congress’s remedial design, effectively converting CDP review into a refund/credit-offset forum despite the traditional refund-suit framework and jurisdictional limits. Precedent counsels methodological consistency: where the challenged government action has ceased and no court-ordered change in legal status within the cause of action remains available, the case is moot.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: This case is not moot because a § 6330(d)(1) petition challenges the Appeals determination regarding the taxpayer’s “unpaid tax” and, where properly raised, the “underlying liability,” and those disputes remain live even if the IRS later abandons the specific levy after collecting through offsets. Under Article III, a case becomes moot only when it is “impossible for a court to grant any effectual relief whatever,” and a judgment that resolves entitlement to the disputed credits/payments—affecting the parties’ legal rights and having concrete practical consequences, including in a related refund action—can constitute effectual relief. Reed v. Goertz and Chafin confirm that even modest, legally operative relief (including judgments with real-world consequences) defeats mootness. Reading § 6330 to permit strategic mootness by switching collection mechanisms would undermine procedural fairness and Congress’s CDP review scheme, while § 6330(e)(1) confirms meaningful remedial authority in respect of the unpaid tax/proposed levy.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a taxpayer’s Tax Court case under 26 U.S.C. § 6330 challenging a proposed IRS levy becomes moot once the levy is no longer being pursued because the IRS collected the disputed amount through offsets or other means.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 26 U.S.C. § 6330 (Collection Due Process—notice and hearing before levy; judicial review under § 6330(d)(1); stay/injunction provisions under § 6330(e)); relatedly, the Declaratory Judgment Act’s tax exception and refund-suit channeling under 26 U.S.C. § 7422 are implicated in the remedies/mootness analysis.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Commissioner argues the § 6330 proceeding is limited to a pre-deprivation review of a specific proposed levy; once the IRS no longer seeks that levy (because the collection dispute over the levy is no longer live), there is no effective relief the Tax Court can provide within § 6330, so the case is moot and continuing it would improperly expand Tax Court jurisdiction into reviewing offsets/collection outcomes or adjudicating liability absent an active levy controversy.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Zuch argues the case is not moot because § 6330(d)(1) authorizes the Tax Court to review the Appeals determination and decide issues like the taxpayer’s unpaid tax and (when properly raised) underlying tax liability, and that controversy remains live even if the IRS drops the levy after collecting through offsets; a Tax Court decision would have real-world consequences by determining who is entitled to the disputed funds, increasing the likelihood of a refund and/or having preclusive effect in a pending or future refund suit under § 7422, and § 6330(e) supports the court’s ability to enter effective relief (including declaratory-type determinations) notwithstanding the usual tax bar on declaratory judgments.
key_precedents: Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020)
Medtronic, Inc. v. Mirowski Family Ventures, LLC, 571 U.S. 191 (2014)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Sotomayor make the best case that vacating an Appeals “determination” could have concrete downstream consequences in a later § 7422 refund suit through issue preclusion, and that Reed v. Goertz/Chafin counsel against mootness when some effectual relief remains. But I agree with Justice Kagan and Justice Alito that Article III redressability must be tied to relief this CDP proceeding can itself award, and § 6330’s text and remedial structure are levy-centric—once the proposed levy is abandoned and collection has proceeded by offsets, the Tax Court cannot in this case alter the parties’ present legal relationship without converting CDP review into a surrogate refund/declaratory action Congress channeled elsewhere. Reed is distinguishable because the requested order there had operative effect in the same litigation (access to DNA testing), whereas here the asserted benefit is chiefly improved odds or preclusion leverage in different litigation—too close to the advisory-opinion concern Spencer identifies. I would therefore hold the case moot on these facts, while leaving open that Congress can address strategic tool-switching or that a different posture (where levy relief remains available) could yield a different result.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s best point is textual: § 6330(d)(1) authorizes review of an Appeals “determination,” and a merits ruling might carry issue-preclusive consequences in a later § 7422 refund suit, invoking Reed v. Goertz. But the original public meaning of § 6330, read as a whole, makes the “determination” reviewable only in the context of a pre-levy check—“before levy” and the stay of “the levy” in § 6330(e) confirm Congress designed effectual relief to be prospective and levy-centered, not an adjudication meant to shape post-collection refund litigation. Reed is distinguishable because the relief there operated directly on the parties’ entitlement in that very proceeding, whereas here the remaining asserted benefit is downstream litigation leverage in a separate cause of action—precisely the sort of collateral, precedent-seeking consequence Spencer v. Kemna treats as insufficient for Article III. Chief Justice Roberts is right that accepting “preclusion-only” redressability would functionally convert CDP into a surrogate refund forum, expanding jurisdiction beyond what Congress enacted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that vacatur of the Appeals “determination” could have concrete downstream monetary consequences through issue preclusion or by materially shaping a later § 7422 refund action, invoking Reed v. Goertz and Church of Scientology. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 6330’s text and remedial design are levy-centric—"before levy" review and a stay tied to “the levy” in § 6330(e)—so once the proposed levy is withdrawn and the Government has collected via offset, the Tax Court cannot grant effectual relief within this CDP proceeding without converting it into a surrogate refund forum Congress routed to § 7422. Reed is distinguishable because the relief there directly operated on an ongoing entitlement in the same case; here the remaining benefit is primarily litigation leverage in a separate action, which Spencer/Knox treat as insufficient to sustain Article III jurisdiction when the statute provides no operative remedy in this posture. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about strategic tool-switching is a legitimate policy worry, but it cannot justify expanding jurisdiction and remedies beyond the scheme Congress enacted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the strongest mootness point: § 6330 is levy-centered and the Tax Court cannot itself order money returned, so once the levy is withdrawn the CDP case purportedly lacks effectual relief. But as Justice Barrett explains, § 6330(d)(1) authorizes judicial review of the Appeals “determination” itself (including properly raised liability or payment-application questions), and vacating or setting aside that determination concretely alters the parties’ legal rights in an ongoing pocketbook dispute—an effect that is materially more than “litigation leverage” under Spencer because it bears directly on what the Government may lawfully retain and what the taxpayer is owed. Reed v. Goertz and Chafin counsel against finding mootness where a merits judgment can still have legally operative consequences that structure the parties’ next steps, even if the ultimate monetary transfer occurs through a different statutory vehicle like § 7422. Pragmatically, adopting Petitioners’ rule would let the IRS moot congressionally mandated CDP review by switching from levy to offset midstream, a real-world impact that undermines access to justice for taxpayers least able to navigate duplicative procedural channels.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that § 6330(d)(1) speaks in terms of reviewing an Appeals “determination,” and that a merits ruling could have concrete issue-preclusive consequences in a later § 7422 refund suit under Reed v. Goertz/Chafin. But Article III redressability has to be anchored to effectual relief the court can grant in this proceeding, and—consistent with Chief Justice Roberts’ and Justice Alito’s levy-centric framing—§ 6330’s text and remedial architecture (including the “before levy” hearing and the § 6330(e) stay of “the levy”) contemplate prospective control over a proposed levy, not post-collection adjudication that functions mainly as litigation leverage elsewhere. Reed is distinguishable because the order there directly governed the plaintiff’s access to DNA testing in the same case; here, once the levy is withdrawn and collection proceeds by offset, the Tax Court cannot undo the completed collection or order a return of funds, leaving only collateral advantage that Spencer cautions is insufficient to keep jurisdiction alive. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about IRS tool-switching is real as a policy matter, but a pragmatic textualist reading keeps CDP coherent as a pre-levy check and channels post-payment relief to § 7422 rather than converting § 6330 review into a surrogate refund forum.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s textual point about review of an Appeals “determination” under § 6330(d)(1), including preserved liability issues under § 6330(c)(2), is the strongest argument against mootness, and I take it seriously. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, the CDP cause of action Congress created is remedially levy-centric—“before levy,” a stay of “the levy” in § 6330(e), and no statutory authority in this proceeding to order return of funds collected by offset—so once the levy is withdrawn the court cannot grant effectual relief within this case without converting CDP review into a surrogate refund forum Congress routed to § 7422. Reed v. Goertz, invoked by Justices Barrett and Jackson, does not move me because the “increased likelihood” there flowed from an order with immediate operative effect in the same case; here the remaining value is principally downstream preclusion/litigation leverage, which Spencer cautions is not enough to avoid an advisory opinion when the present proceeding cannot alter the parties’ legal relationship. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about strategic mooting is a real policy problem, but under Article III and the statute’s best reading, the remedy lies in the refund path (or Congress), not in expanding § 6330 beyond its original design.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that § 6330(d)(1) speaks in terms of reviewing the Appeals “determination,” and that a merits ruling could have legally operative, potentially preclusive effects in a later § 7422 refund suit under Reed v. Goertz’s “increased likelihood” framing. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Article III redressability must be anchored to effectual relief the court can award in this CDP proceeding, and § 6330’s text and remedial structure are levy-centric (including § 6330(e)’s stay of “the levy”), with no authority here to unwind completed offsets or order return of funds. Reed and Church of Scientology are distinguishable because the relief there directly altered the parties’ present legal relationship in the same case, whereas “preclusion-only” or “litigation advantage later” relief risks the advisory-opinion problem Spencer v. Kemna warns against and would effectively convert CDP into a surrogate refund forum Congress channeled to § 7422. Justice Sotomayor’s strategic-mooting concern is serious as a practical matter, but under an institutionalist, statute-respecting approach the fix lies with Congress or a case where levy relief remains available, not by expanding § 6330 jurisdiction beyond its designed lane.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the core objection that § 6330 is levy-centric and that, once the levy is withdrawn and the Tax Court cannot order a refund, any remaining benefit is merely “downstream litigation advantage” forbidden by Spencer. But § 6330(d)(1)’s text authorizes judicial review of the Appeals “determination,” and when the taxpayer properly raises the “underlying tax liability” under § 6330(c)(2), setting aside that determination alters the parties’ legal relationship in a concrete, legally operative way—much closer to Church of Scientology’s effectual-relief principle than Spencer’s speculative collateral consequences. Reed v. Goertz reinforces that relief need not be immediate; vacatur or correction of the determination can materially govern the parties’ rights in the inevitable refund posture, and I do not read Article III or the statute to permit unilateral mooting by the Government’s midstream switch of collection tools. Justice Kavanaugh’s advisory-opinion concern is serious, but it rests on treating preclusion as “mere precedent,” whereas here the challenged determination is the operative agency act Congress made reviewable and its legal consequences persist beyond the abandoned levy.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the hardest point: § 6330 is levy-centric, and once the levy is withdrawn and collection proceeds by offset, continuing the case risks turning CDP review into a surrogate refund forum Congress routed to § 7422. But I agree with Justice Barrett (and Justice Sotomayor) that Article III mootness turns on whether any effectual relief remains, and § 6330(d)(1) authorizes judicial review of the Appeals “determination” itself—so vacatur or merits correction can still concretely alter the parties’ legal rights by removing legally operative determinations that would otherwise bind (or materially structure) the inevitable refund/credit-application dispute. Reed v. Goertz and Chafin undercut the premise that only immediate, same-proceeding monetary relief counts; here the consequence is not Spencer’s speculative stigma but a direct, pocketbook-impacting preclusive effect concerning whether the Government may retain the money it has already taken. Pragmatically, adopting petitioners’ mootness rule would invite the IRS to defeat Congress’s stay-and-review scheme by switching collection tools midstream, undermining procedural fairness in precisely the setting § 6330 was designed to regulate.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 6330 establishes a narrowly focused, pre-levy review mechanism: it requires notice and a hearing “before levy,” provides a stay while that levy is at issue, and authorizes Tax Court review of the Appeals determination in that collection posture. Once the IRS is no longer pursuing the challenged levy because the amount has been collected through offsets, it is “impossible for a court to grant any effectual relief” within the confines of § 6330, satisfying the mootness standard articulated in Knox v. SEIU and applied in Chafin v. Chafin. The taxpayer’s interest in potential preclusion or improved prospects in a later refund suit does not supply the requisite live controversy here; Article III mootness generally is not avoided by collateral litigation advantages, and Congress has channeled post-payment recovery into refund procedures under 26 U.S.C. § 7422 rather than converting § 6330 into a declaratory/refund forum. A narrow holding finding mootness in these circumstances best respects statutory limits and institutional legitimacy while leaving the taxpayer to the remedy Congress provided.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 6330 is textually framed as a pre-levy procedural protection—"notice and opportunity for hearing" before a levy—and the judicial review it authorizes in § 6330(d)(1) is tied to that collection determination; once the IRS is no longer pursuing the levy, a court order setting aside that levy affords no operative relief. Any further adjudication of underlying liability to influence potential refunds or future § 7422 litigation would exceed § 6330’s limited grant and amount to an advisory opinion barred by Article III, because any refund remedy must proceed through the refund-suit channel Congress prescribed. Potential preclusive effect or increased likelihood of a later refund is not the kind of redressability that sustains a live controversy where the only statutorily cognizable action (the levy) has disappeared. Consistent with this Court’s insistence that federal courts decide only live disputes with effective relief available, the case becomes moot when the challenged levy is off the table.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 6330 is textually structured as pre-levy process—notice, a hearing, and judicial review of an Appeals determination concerning whether the IRS may proceed “with the proposed levy,” with a stay keyed to that levy under § 6330(e); once the IRS is no longer pursuing the levy because it has collected via offsets or other means, the court cannot grant effectual relief within the CDP/levy framework. Whatever the taxpayer’s continuing interest in getting money back is channeled into the refund-suit regime in 26 U.S.C. § 7422 (and the tax exception to declaratory relief underscores Congress’s general remedial design), so keeping a § 6330 case alive to obtain a merits ruling that might aid a later refund action would improperly expand Tax Court jurisdiction beyond the live levy controversy. Under Article III principles, a case is moot when it is “impossible for a court to grant any effectual relief whatever,” Knox v. SEIU, 567 U.S. 298, 307 (2012), and the possibility of issue preclusion or a tactical advantage in future litigation is not itself effectual relief. Practical consequences also counsel against allowing taxpayers to transform CDP review into a general vehicle for adjudicating liability after collection has occurred, which would undermine the statutory channels Congress provided for post-collection disputes.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A § 6330(d)(1) case is moot only if it is impossible to grant any effectual relief, and that is not true where the Tax Court can still determine whether the IRS properly applied the taxpayer’s prepayments/estimated payments to the asserted liability—an outcome that affects whether the IRS must return the disputed funds. Even if the IRS abandons the particular levy after collecting via offsets, the parties retain a concrete stake because the Tax Court’s determination can materially shape entitlement to money and carry preclusive consequences in a refund suit channeled through § 7422, which is a classic collateral consequence preserving a live controversy. Under Chafin v. Chafin, a continuing “concrete interest, however small,” defeats mootness, and Reed v. Goertz reinforces that a case remains live where a court can still provide meaningful, practical relief. Reading § 6330 narrowly to permit the IRS to moot judicial review by switching collection tools would undermine Congress’s protective, pre-deprivation review scheme for taxpayers—especially those least able to navigate parallel litigation paths—and would erode fair access to judicial oversight.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 6330 is structured as a Collection Due Process regime providing pre-levy process and judicial review of an Appeals “determination” about whether a proposed levy may proceed; once the IRS is no longer pursuing that levy and the tax has been collected by offsets, the Tax Court cannot grant the core relief the statute contemplates—relief from levy—so the controversy is no longer redressable within § 6330(d)(1). Treating a continuing desire for a liability ruling (to improve odds in a later refund suit) as sufficient would make § 6330 an end-run around Congress’s channeling of post-payment disputes into refund actions under § 7422 and would press against the tax exception to declaratory relief; Article III does not permit keeping a case alive for “preclusion-only” benefits. Consistent with workability and statutory coherence, mootness avoids converting a narrowly targeted collection-review mechanism into a roving liability or overpayment forum once collection by levy is off the table. This aligns with the D.C. Circuit’s approach in Willson v. Comm’r, which correctly reads § 6330’s remedies as levy-focused rather than an open-ended vehicle for declaratory determinations untethered to an ongoing collection action.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 6330 is textually framed around a specific “proposed levy” and provides for review of the Appeals “determination” in that levy proceeding; once the IRS is no longer pursuing the levy and has already collected via offsets, it becomes impossible for the Tax Court to grant “effectual relief” within the remedial lane Congress specified for § 6330, rendering the case moot under Knox v. SEIU. Any remaining interest in improving prospects in a separate refund action under § 7422 (or in potential issue-preclusion) is a collateral consequence that does not itself supply Article III adversity for the § 6330 case, and allowing it would risk expanding Tax Court jurisdiction beyond the separation-of-powers limits Congress set. Section 6330(e)’s stay/injunction mechanism reinforces that Congress contemplated prospective relief tied to preventing a levy, not adjudicating entitlement to money already collected by other means. The taxpayer’s remedy for recovery of collected funds lies in the refund-suit channeling scheme, not by keeping a levy-review case alive after the levy is off the table.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 6330 is structured as a targeted, pre-levy process: it requires notice and a hearing “before levy,” provides for judicial review of the Appeals determination, and in § 6330(e) stays “the levy” while that review is pending—signaling that the court’s remedial authority is tied to an ongoing levy controversy rather than post-collection reallocations. Once the IRS is no longer pursuing the levy and has already collected through offsets, it becomes “impossible for a court to grant any effectual relief whatever” within the § 6330 proceeding, because the Tax Court cannot order a refund and Congress has channeled refund relief through § 7422, consistent with the tax system’s traditional limits on declaratory-type relief. Unlike Church of Scientology v. United States, 506 U.S. 9 (1992), where the Court could still grant meaningful relief by ordering return or destruction of wrongfully obtained materials, the asserted “collateral consequences” here (potential persuasive or preclusive effects in a future refund suit) resemble the insufficient, speculative consequences rejected in Spencer v. Kemna, 523 U.S. 1 (1998). Respect for statutory design, history, and practical workability counsels against expanding § 6330 into a general vehicle for litigating post-collection entitlement once the levy itself is off the table.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 6330(d)(1) authorizes judicial review of the Appeals “determination,” and § 6330(c)(2) permits the taxpayer (when properly raised) to contest the underlying liability; nothing in that text makes the Tax Court’s jurisdiction evaporate simply because the IRS later collects the amount through offsets rather than the proposed levy. Under Article III mootness principles, a case remains live when a court can grant effective relief by changing the parties’ legal rights, and a Tax Court judgment resolving entitlement to the disputed payments would materially increase the likelihood of a refund and would have concrete collateral consequences through issue preclusion in a § 7422 refund suit. Reed v. Goertz confirms that relief is not moot where a favorable judgment would “increase the likelihood” of the downstream remedy, and Herrera v. Wyoming underscores that issue preclusion is a real legal consequence sufficient to keep an otherwise-ended dispute from becoming academic. Treating the case as moot merely because the IRS shifted collection mechanisms would also allow the Government to defeat § 6330 review through unilateral action, contrary to the statute’s design to provide judicial review of the determination before collection becomes irreversible.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: A § 6330(d)(1) case is not moot merely because the IRS stops pursuing the specific levy after collecting through offsets, so long as the taxpayer retains a concrete stake and the court can grant effectual relief—here, a determination bearing on the unpaid tax and/or properly raised underlying liability that would likely redress a pocketbook injury by affecting entitlement to the disputed funds. Under Reed v. Goertz and Chafin, a case becomes moot only when it is impossible to grant any effectual relief; practical legal consequences, including likely preclusive or channeling effects in a refund suit under § 7422, can suffice for redressability. Section 6330(e)’s stay and related remedial structure reinforce that Congress contemplated meaningful judicial review of the Appeals determination, not jurisdiction that evaporates whenever the IRS changes collection tools midstream. Given procedural fairness concerns and the risk of insulating collection decisions from review, I would hold the controversy remains live notwithstanding the shift from levy to offsets.
